title: The swan
hook: a later telling: cousin Devadatta shoots a swan, Siddhattha tends it, and the court says it belongs to the one who saved it
carry: life belongs to who protects it

segments.voice: Yesterday: jhana, the quiet joy under the rose-apple tree. Your line was you've been here before. Did you find a childhood peace for a breath? Day twenty-eight.

A week of stories. A queen's dream of a white elephant. A birth in a garden on the road. An old sage in tears. A mother lost at seven days, and a mother who stayed. A name that's a wish. A boy at peace under a tree. Today, the last story of the childhood, and it's one that millions of children have heard. Two boys, cousins, in the palace gardens. A flock of swans flies overhead, white against the sky. One of the cousins has a bow. He draws it, and shoots. And a swan falls out of the sky, an arrow through its wing.
screen: `A WEEK OF STORIES.` → `SWANS OVERHEAD.` → `AN ARROW, AND ONE FALLS.`

segments.voice: The cousin with the bow is Devadatta. Remember that name; he'll be back, and not kindly. The swan lands near Siddhattha, who gets there first. He kneels, gently pulls out the arrow, and holds the bird against himself to calm it, tending the wound. Then Devadatta runs up. That's my swan. I shot it. Give it to me. Siddhattha says no. It isn't yours. You tried to kill it. I saved it. The boys can't settle it, so the story goes, they take it to the court, to the wise men. Both sides are heard. The hunter says: I brought it down, so it's mine. The healer says: I kept it alive, so it's in my care. And the court decides: a life belongs to the one who saves it, not the one who tries to take it. The swan goes with Siddhattha, who looks after it until it can fly, and then lets it go. It's worth being honest about this one. The swan story isn't in the oldest Buddhist texts. It's a later telling, and it became famous in the West through a long English poem, The Light of Asia, published by Edwin Arnold in eighteen seventy-nine. But it's loved across the Buddhist world, in picture books and school plays and temple paintings, because it says something the whole tradition believes. The first precept, remember, is not to harm living beings. Here it is in a child, before anyone taught him. And look at the judgment. Not might makes right. Care makes right. Life belongs to who protects it.
screen: `DEVADATTA SHOOTS. SIDDHATTHA KNEELS.` · `THAT'S MY SWAN.` · `THE COURT: IT'S THE SAVER'S.` · `A LATER TELLING, WIDELY LOVED.` · then, large: `LIFE BELONGS TO WHO PROTECTS IT.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. Think of one small living thing you could care for today. A plant that needs water. A pet. A bird feeder that's empty. An insect in the house you could carry outside instead of swatting. Picture yourself doing it, slowly, with the same gentle hands the boy used with the swan. Then rest in the breath, and let a little metta go to that small life. The bell holds the time.
The swan. Devadatta shot it, Siddhattha saved it, and the court said a life belongs to the one who protects it.
Your line: life belongs to who protects it. Today, actually do it: care for one small living thing, and do it gently. Day twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Buddhists tell the swan story to children as an example of compassion toward animals; many Buddhists practice releasing or protecting animals, and some keep a vegetarian diet out of the same concern for living beings.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali: a swan or goose, a common image of purity and grace in Indian traditions.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sweet story about a boy and a bird.
what it means: the first precept, not harming living beings, shown in a child, and a judgment that care, not force, gives the right to a life.

what a scholar hears: the story isn't in the Pali canon; it's told in later biographies and was popularized in English by Edwin Arnold's The Light of Asia (1879). Devadatta's rivalry here foreshadows his later schism.

sources.ref: later biographies of the Buddha; Edwin Arnold, The Light of Asia (1879), Book the First
